summaries.example: You must choose between taking a bus that will probably arrive soon and a taxi that costs more but is more likely to be quick. You think about what might happen, how likely each result is, and how much you care about each result. Decision theory studies this kind of careful choosing.
summaries.summary: Decision theory asks how a person should reason when choosing among options. It studies preferences—what a person sees as better or worse—and beliefs about what may happen. In the usual expected-utility approach, a person considers each possible result, how likely it is, and how desirable it is according to that person. The approach uses utility functions to represent preferences. An ordinal utility function records only the order of choices, such as first, second, and third. A richer cardinal utility function also represents differences between choices by using preferences over lotteries, or chance-based choices. Philosophers disagree about whether people must always be able to compare every pair of options and whether preferences must always fit the rules of transitivity and independence. Some examples, such as choices involving regret or a very small chance of disaster, put pressure on the standard theory. The entry also compares different ways to represent uncertainty and explains why choices made over time can be harder than one-time choices.
key_ideas: Decision theory studies the reasoning behind choices, including ordinary choices and very important choices.
A preference compares options: one may seem better, worse, or just as good as another.
Rational preferences are often described as complete and transitive, though philosophers debate whether these rules always fit real choices.
Expected utility combines how good an outcome is with how likely it is.
Numbers can represent preferences, but they do not automatically show an absolute amount of happiness or allow simple comparisons between different people.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make choices with incomplete information every day. Decision theory gives us tools for thinking clearly about chances, goals, and trade-offs. It also shows that being a careful chooser is not always simple: rules that seem sensible in one situation may seem less convincing in another. These ideas matter in personal decisions, science, economics, public policy, and discussions about what people value.

important_terms.definition: A choice or action that someone can consider, such as taking a bus or a taxi.
A way of saying which option someone likes better, likes less, or likes equally.
A number used to show how desirable an option is for a particular person.
Not knowing exactly what will happen. A person may use beliefs about how likely different results are.
A rule saying that, when outcomes are uncertain, we should choose the option with the greatest average value after considering the chances.

Can a choice be reasonable even if it does not have the highest expected result?
Why might two people give different utility numbers to the same prize?
Should a tiny chance of a very bad result always matter in the same way?

summaries.example: Suppose a student can accept a guaranteed moderate scholarship or enter a competition with a 20% chance of a much larger scholarship and an 80% chance of receiving nothing. Expected utility does not simply compare the dollar amounts. It compares the utilities of the outcomes and weights them by their probabilities. A student who chooses differently may have different preferences about risk, or may reject one of the theory’s assumptions, such as Independence.
summaries.summary: Decision theory investigates the reasoning underlying an agent’s choices, with normative decision theory asking which structures preferences and related attitudes should have. Its central problem is choice under uncertainty. Orthodox expected utility theory says that an agent should prefer the option whose possible outcomes have the highest probability-weighted desirability, measured from the agent’s perspective. The theory begins with preferences over prospects and commonly assumes a weak preference relation that is complete and transitive. Completeness requires comparison of every pair; transitivity rules out preference cycles. Both assumptions are contested, especially for heterogeneous options or cases involving several dimensions of value. Utility functions represent preference orderings. Ordinal utilities encode rank alone and cannot support meaningful averaging across lotteries. Cardinal, or interval-valued, utilities encode relative differences and are unique up to positive linear transformation. They do not provide absolute utility and, without extra assumptions, are not interpersonally comparable. The von Neumann–Morgenstern theorem shows that preferences over suitably rich lotteries can be represented as maximizing expected utility when they satisfy ordering, Continuity, and Independence conditions. Continuity can seem implausible when catastrophic outcomes are involved, while Independence is challenged by the Allais pattern, in which people’s preferences appear sensitive to a common outcome or to regret. key_ideas: Normative decision theory offers a minimal account of rationality: it mainly concerns coherence among preferences, beliefs, and values rather than deciding which desires are morally or substantively correct.
Expected utility theory recommends the option with the greatest probability-weighted desirability.
Ordinal utility represents ranking only. Cardinal utility is richer and is constructed through preferences over lotteries; its scale is fixed only up to a positive linear transformation.
The vNM representation theorem links expected-utility maximization to preference axioms including Completeness, Transitivity, Continuity, and Independence.

Savage separates states of the world, outcomes, and acts in order to derive both a probability representation of belief and a utility representation of desire. Jeffrey instead evaluates propositions using conditional probabilities and does not require the same act-state separation.
Challenges include Allais-style violations of Independence, incomplete or imprecise preferences, catastrophic risk, unawareness, and the difficulty of representing choices that unfold over time.
summaries.why_it_matters: Decision theory connects practical rationality with theories of belief and value. It helps explain how probability and preference can guide action, why gathering information may be valuable, and why inconsistent attitudes can produce self-defeating choices. At the same time, its limits are philosophically important: a model may depend on how options and outcomes are described, may struggle with vague beliefs or incomparable values, and may give different advice about risk, regret, catastrophe, and future changes in preference. Studying these disagreements clarifies what mathematical representation can—and cannot—tell us about rational agency.

important_terms.definition: A relation comparing options according to how desirable or choice-worthy an agent takes them to be.
An entity capable of deliberating and acting; in decision theory, usually an individual person.
A numerical representation of preference. Ordinal utility records ranking; cardinal utility also represents relevant differences between values.
A preference relation is complete when every pair of options can be compared, at least weakly.
A preference relation is transitive when preferring or weakly preferring A to B and B to C supports preferring A to C.
The weighted sum of the utilities of possible outcomes, where each utility is multiplied by its probability.
In vNM theory, the condition that a common outcome should not change the preference between two lotteries when its probability is held fixed.
A decision situation in which outcomes have probabilities, or in which the agent’s beliefs supply probabilities for possible states.

questions_to_think_about: Is Completeness a genuine requirement of rationality, or can two options be genuinely incomparable?
Does a money-pump argument show that intransitive preferences are irrational, or only that they can lead to costly behavior under particular assumptions?
Are Allais preferences irrational, or do they reveal that the standard description of outcomes leaves out regret or context?
Should beliefs be represented by one precise probability function when evidence is vague?
What should a decision theory recommend when a person’s future preferences will differ from present preferences?

summaries.example: Imagine choosing between two after-school plans. Plan A definitely gives you one hour to play with friends. Plan B gives you a 70% chance of two hours and a 30% chance of having to help clean the gym. To decide, you consider both your chances and how much you value each possible result. Another student might choose differently because the cleaning outcome matters more to them or because they dislike risk.
summaries.summary: Decision theory is the study of reasoning about choices. It examines ordinary decisions, such as choosing transportation, as well as choices with broad effects. An agent’s preferences compare options by their desirability or choice-worthiness. The standard normative approach asks which patterns of preference are rational without settling every question about what a person ought to want or believe. The most familiar rule is expected utility: when several results are possible, consider how desirable each result is and how likely it is, then favor the option with the greatest weighted total. To represent preferences, theorists use utility functions. An ordinal utility function records only which options come before others. A cardinal utility function contains more information about the relative gaps between options. Lotteries help construct this richer scale: if someone is indifferent between a middle option and a lottery combining a best and worst option, the chance assigned to the best outcome can represent the middle option’s position. The von Neumann–Morgenstern theorem says that, for an appropriate set of lotteries, expected-utility representation follows from several conditions. Completeness and Transitivity provide an ordering; Continuity connects intermediate options with suitable chances; Independence says common outcomes should not affect comparisons. These conditions are influential but disputed. Many people show Allais-type preferences that favor certainty in one comparison but accept extra risk in another, apparently violating Independence. key_ideas: Decision theory studies both what people choose and the beliefs, desires, and preferences that help explain those choices.
Expected utility theory says to favor the option with the highest expected desirability when outcomes are uncertain.
Ordinal utility tells us only the order of preferences. Cardinal utility also represents the relative size of differences, using lotteries to build a scale.
Philosophers debate whether completeness and transitivity should always be required, especially when options involve different kinds of value.
The vNM theorem explains when preferences over lotteries can be represented by expected utility, but examples such as the Allais paradox challenge one of its important assumptions.
Savage and Jeffrey offer different ways to connect preferences with beliefs about uncertain situations.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject matters because choices are shaped by both goals and uncertainty. Decision theory gives a precise language for discussing risk, evidence, trade-offs, and consistency. It also teaches an important lesson about models: a rule may work well for one kind of decision but fit poorly when people care about regret, face vague evidence, cannot imagine all possibilities, or must make a series of choices. Understanding these limits helps us evaluate arguments instead of treating a formula as an unquestionable answer.

important_terms.definition: A comparison in which one option is judged at least as good as, better than, or equal to another.
A person or other decision-maker who can think about choices and act.
A number used to represent how desirable an option is for an agent.
The rule that every pair of options can be compared in some way.
The rule that if A is at least as good as B, and B is at least as good as C, then A is at least as good as C.
The value of possible results multiplied by their chances and then added together.
A chance-based option, such as a game or lottery with different possible prizes.
A requirement that a shared part of two lotteries should not change the comparison between their differing parts.

questions_to_think_about: If you cannot decide between two options, does that mean your thinking is irrational?
Why is a ranking like first, second, third not enough to compare two lotteries?
Can a person dislike risk without making a mistake?
How could regret change the way someone evaluates a chance-based choice?
Is choosing now while predicting a different future choice always irrational?
